title: Study Abroad Experience at the Medical University of Gdansk
paragraphs: I was allowed to experience three months of clinical clerkships at the Medical University of Gdansk. I had been very interested in the exchange program even before I entered university, and I am deeply moved that my long-held wish has come true. There were two main reasons I chose the Medical University of Gdansk: one was that I thought the "English Division" system would let me do clerkships in English even while in Europe, and the other was that I thought studying medicine in a non-English-speaking country like Poland would be very difficult in the future and that this was my last chance. Now, as I write this account of my study abroad, I keenly feel that my choice was not mistaken, and I also realize anew that it was a study abroad life supported by many people. With apologies for my presumption, I would now like to write about my life abroad.

Because I was interested in surgical fields, I put together my own clerkship program centered on surgical fields. Specifically, I rotated through various departments in the following rotation: obstetrics and gynecology (3 weeks), rehabilitation (2 weeks), neonatology (1 week), general surgery (2 weeks) and family medicine (3 weeks). Since it had been formally incorporated into the English Division program from last year, I took part in each clerkship with the local students, and, as with the local students, I would not receive credit unless I passed the written examination (oral examination) on the last day of each department, but thanks to the examinations I think I was given the chance to study together with the local students and to learn about diseases that are hard to see in Japan. The roots of the local students are very diverse, with students from Sweden and Saudi Arabia in particular, from neighboring countries such as Spain, Italy, Germany and Slovakia, and also from the United States and India. But students from Asia seem very rare, and in every group the Japanese were very well received, and thanks to being warmly welcomed I think I was able to lead a fulfilling clerkship life. Among them, obstetrics and gynecology stays most in my heart, so let me write about it briefly.

The hospital with obstetrics and gynecology was about a 30-minute walk from our dormitory, and was good morning exercise. In this clerkship I was with fifth-year students, and I often acted together with an Italian female student, and we often talked about each other's countries and our futures. My supervising doctor was Dr. Adamski of obstetrics, a doctor over two meters tall, who was very enthusiastic about teaching and even held a special class on childbirth on a Saturday when there was no clerkship. He was also very witty, and jokes like "I don't like sleep, so I'm an obstetrician" and "For the operation, the most important preparation is lunch. No food, no operation!" were brilliant. In the clerkship I was allowed to observe the natural delivery of a pregnant woman with a BMI over 50, including measurement of the Bishop score, a very valuable experience.

The three months in Poland, blessed with the best friends and a partner, I feel were the most intense and fulfilling days of my life. Although my English did not visibly improve and I did not visibly acquire medical knowledge or skills, I can declare that I was able to experience many things that I could not have learned just by doing clerkships in Japan. From now on I intend to make the most of what I learned in Poland and work even harder so that I can become a useful doctor.

Finally, I would like to thank again all the people who have been involved not only in this exchange but also in the exchange between Nagoya University and the Medical University of Gdansk until now. Thank you.
